URL: An Amazon EC2 instance is a virtual server in the AWS Cloud environment. Users have full control over an instance from the time it is launched until it is terminated. Instances can run a variety of operating systems and can be configured after launch by installing software, updates, and applications. An instance is launched from an AMI (Amazon Machine Image) into a selected AWS Region and Availability Zone. Once launched, the instance transitions through a lifecycle of states: pending, running, stopping, stopped, and terminated. Billing begins when the instance enters the running state and stops when it transitions to shutting down during termination. Stopping an instance pauses billing; starting it again resumes billing. Instances can be managed directly or as managed instances, where a service provider such as Amazon EKS Auto Mode controls the instance settings. Managed instances cannot be directly modified and are identified by a true value in the Managed field. URL: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) provides on-demand, scalable computing capacity in the AWS Cloud. It reduces hardware costs and allows faster application development and deployment. Using EC2, you can launch as many or as few virtual servers as needed, configure security and networking, and manage storage. An EC2 instance is a virtual server in the AWS Cloud. The instance type specified at launch determines the hardware available to that instance. Each instance type offers a different balance of compute, memory, network, and storage resources. EC2 instances are launched from Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), which are preconfigured templates that include the operating system and any additional software. Once launched, an instance transitions to a running state and billing begins. Billing stops when the instance is stopped or terminated. URL: Amazon EC2 offers multiple purchasing and billing options to allow users to optimize cost based on usage patterns, commitment level, and workload characteristics. All billing options use per-second billing with a minimum charge of 60 seconds. EC2 usage is billed in one-second increments with a 60-second minimum. This applies to all purchasing options, all Regions, and all Availability Zones. The same per-second billing applies to provisioned Amazon EBS storage. Billing starts when an instance enters the running state and stops when the instance terminates or stops. Pay by the second for instances that are launched with no long-term commitment. The price per second is fixed and listed on the EC2 On-Demand pricing page. Recommended for short-term, irregular workloads that cannot be interrupted. On-Demand quotas are managed in terms of vCPUs per AWS account per Region. Reduce costs by committing to a consistent usage amount measured in USD per hour for a term of 1 or 3 years. It controls who is authenticated (signed in) and authorized (has permissions) to use resources. IAM provides the infrastructure necessary to control authentication and authorization for AWS accounts. IAM, AWS IAM Identity Center, and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) are offered at no additional charge. URL: A policy is an object in AWS that, when associated with an identity or resource, defines their permissions. AWS evaluates these policies when an IAM principal (user or role) makes a request. Permissions in the policies determine whether the request is allowed or denied. Most policies are stored in AWS as JSON documents. When a principal makes a request, AWS evaluates all applicable policies. The default result for any request is an implicit deny. An explicit allow in an identity-based or resource-based policy overrides this default. An explicit deny in any policy overrides any allow. If a permissions boundary, AWS Organizations SCP, or session policy is present, all of those policies must also allow the request. IAM policy evaluation uses an explicit deny model, meaning a single denied action causes the entire request to be denied. Policies define permissions by specifying: the actions allowed or denied, the resources those actions apply to, and any conditions under which the policy applies. IAM policies are written in the IAM JSON policy language. AWS supports seven types of policies: JSON policy documents attached to an IAM identity (user, group, or role). URLs: IAM identities are the entities created in an AWS account to provide access to AWS resources for people and processes. IAM identities include IAM users, IAM groups, and IAM roles. Each identity can be associated with one or more policies that determine what actions it is authorized to perform, on which resources, and under what conditions. An IAM user is an identity within an AWS account that has specific permissions for a single person or application. IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords (for console access) or access keys (for programmatic access). By default, a newly created IAM user has no permissions. AWS recommends using IAM users only for use cases that are not supported by federation, including workloads that cannot use IAM roles and tools that require long-term access keys. Root user: When an AWS account is created, it begins with a root user that has complete access to all services and resources. AWS strongly recommends not using the root user for everyday tasks. Use IAM users or roles instead. An IAM group is a collection of IAM users. Policies attached to a group apply to all users in that group. Groups simplify permission management for users

using the root user for everyday tasks. Use IAM users or roles instead. An IAM group is a collection of IAM users. Policies attached to a group apply to all users in that group. Groups simplify permission management for users who require the same level of access. An IAM role is an IAM identity within an AWS account that has specific permissions. Unlike an IAM user, a role is not associated with a single person. A role is intended to be assumable by anyone or any service that needs it. Roles do not have long-term credentials such as passwords or static access keys. Instead, assuming a role provides temporary security credentials for the duration of the session. A role has two types of policies attached: - Trust policy: A resource-based policy that defines which principals (accounts, users, roles, and AWS services) are trusted to assume the role. This is a required policy. - Permissions policy: An identity-based policy that defines what actions and resources the role can access after it is assumed. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is an object storage service that provides scalable storage over the internet. It is designed to store and retrieve any amount of data from anywhere at any time. Data is stored as objects within containers called buckets. Users create a bucket in a selected AWS region. Each object stored in a bucket consists of the data itself, a unique key (identifier), and metadata. Objects can range in size from a few bytes up to 5 terabytes. S3 does not use a traditional file system hierarchy; instead, it uses a flat structure where each object is accessed via a unique URL or API call. Access is managed through bucket policies, access control lists (ACLs), and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. - Virtually unlimited storage capacity with no minimum commitment - High durability: S3 is designed for 99.999999999 percent (11 nines) durability by redundantly storing data across multiple facilities - Multiple storage classes available to balance cost and access frequency (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier, etc.) - Versioning support to retain multiple versions of an object - Server-side and client-side encryption options for data security - Lifecycle policies to automate transitions between storage classes or object

to balance cost and access frequency (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier, etc.) - Versioning support to retain multiple versions of an object - Server-side and client-side encryption options for data security - Lifecycle policies to automate transitions between storage classes or object deletion - Event notifications to trigger workflows when objects are created or modified - Cross-region replication for geographic redundancy Backup and disaster recovery: Organizations store critical data backups that can be retrieved reliably when needed. Static website hosting: S3 can serve static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files directly to end users. This document outlines the procedure for requesting, approving, and revoking access to company systems, tools, and data environments. All access requests must be submitted through the IT portal. Requests submitted via email or direct message to IT staff will not be processed. Each request must specify the system or resource, the level of access required, the business justification, and the expected duration if the access is temporary. Access is granted on the principle of least privilege. Employees will be given only the minimum level of access needed to perform their job function. Requests for elevated permissions such as admin or write access to production systems require additional justification and are subject to a secondary approval from the department head. Standard access requests are reviewed and fulfilled within 2 business days. Requests for production or sensitive system access may take up to 5 business days due to the additional approval steps. Urgent access needs may be escalated to IT leadership with manager sign-off, but urgency does not bypass the approval process. Temporary access must include an expiry date. IT will automatically revoke access on the stated date without further notification. If continued access is needed, a new request must be submitted

manager sign-off, but urgency does not bypass the approval process. Temporary access must include an expiry date. IT will automatically revoke access on the stated date without further notification. If continued access is needed, a new request must be submitted before expiry. Access must be reviewed when an employee changes roles internally. The previous access profile must be revoked within 5 business days of the role change taking effect. Managers are responsible for initiating this review. When an employee leaves the company, the manager must notify HR and IT on the last working day. All system access will be revoked within 4 hours of the departure being confirmed. Failure to report a departure promptly is a policy violation.

This document defines the standards all engineers must follow when designing and building internal and external APIs. All APIs must follow REST principles. Endpoints must use noun-based resource naming in lowercase with hyphens as separators. Verbs must not appear in endpoint paths. HTTP methods must be used semantically: GET for retrieval, POST for creation, PUT for full replacement, PATCH for partial update, and DELETE for removal. All API responses must return JSON. Response structures must be consistent across endpoints, with a data field for successful responses and an error field containing a code and message for failures. HTTP status codes must accurately reflect the outcome of the request. Using 200 for error responses is not permitted. All endpoints must be versioned using a URL path prefix such as v1 or v2. Breaking changes must result in a new version. Deprecation of an existing version requires a minimum 90-day notice communicated in the internal changelog and to all known consumers. Authentication is required for all non-public endpoints. OAuth 2.0 with bearer tokens is the standard authentication method. is required for all non-public endpoints. OAuth 2.0 with bearer tokens is the standard authentication method. API keys may be used for internal service-to-service communication and must be rotated every 180 days. Every API must have complete documentation generated from the codebase using the approved specification format. Documentation must include endpoint descriptions, required and optional parameters, example request and response payloads, and error codes. Documentation must be updated as part of the same pull request that introduces the API change. Rate limiting must be applied to all public-facing endpoints. Limits and retry guidance must be communicated through response headers. Input validation must be performed on all request parameters before any processing occurs.

This document defines the standards and expectations for conducting code reviews across all engineering teams. Every code change must be reviewed before merging. Pull requests require a minimum of two approvals from engineers other than the author. At least one reviewer must have familiarity with the part of the codebase being modified. Self-merging without the required approvals is not permitted under any circumstances. Reviewers are expected to respond to a pull request within one business day. If a reviewer cannot complete a review within that time, they must reassign it or notify the author. Authors must address all comments before requesting re-review. Reviewers should check that error handling is explicit, that sensitive data is not logged, and that no hardcoded credentials are present. This document describes the steps required to deploy application changes to staging and production environments. It applies to all backend, frontend, and infrastructure changes. All deployments must originate from a versioned release branch in the main repository. No direct commits to the main or production branch are permitted. Hotfixes are the only exception and must follow the hotfix procedure documented separately. Before a deployment can proceed, the following conditions must be met. The pull request must have been reviewed and approved by at least two engineers. All automated tests in the CI pipeline must pass. The release branch must be synchronized with the latest changes from the main branch. A deployment ticket must be open and linked to the release. Deployments to the staging environment can be initiated by any engineer with deployment access. Staging deployments run automatically via the CI pipeline on merge to the staging branch. Engineers are responsible for verifying behavior in staging before requesting a production deployment. Production deployments require approval from the team lead or release manager. Deployments outside this window require written approval from the engineering manager and must be logged as exceptions. After a production deployment, the deploying engineer must monitor application logs and error tracking dashboards for a minimum of 30 minutes. If anomalies are detected, the rollback procedure must be initiated immediately without waiting for impact confirmation. All deployments, including rollbacks, must be recorded in the deployment log with the engineer name, timestamp, release version, and any post-deployment observations.

This document defines how incidents affecting production systems are identified, escalated, managed, and resolved. It applies to all engineering and operations staff. An incident is any unplanned event that causes or risks causing a degradation or outage of a production service. Incidents are classified into three severity levels. Severity 1 is a complete service outage or data loss affecting all or most users. Severity 2 is a significant degradation affecting a subset of users or a critical feature. Severity 3 is a minor issue with limited user impact or a workaround available. When an incident is detected, the person who identifies it must immediately create an incident ticket in the tracking system, set the severity level, and notify the on-call engineer via the alerting channel. For Severity 1 incidents, the engineering manager and product lead must also be notified within 10 minutes. The on-call engineer assumes the role of incident commander and is responsible for coordinating the response. A dedicated incident channel must be created for Severity 1 and Severity 2 incidents. All investigation and communication must happen in that channel to maintain a clear record. The incident commander assigns tasks, provides status updates every 30 minutes to stakeholders for

incident channel must be created for Severity 1 and Severity 2 incidents. All investigation and communication must happen in that channel to maintain a clear record. The incident commander assigns tasks, provides status updates every 30 minutes to stakeholders for Severity 1, and ensures a resolution path is active at all times. Engineers not assigned a task must not act independently unless directed by the incident commander. Once resolved, the incident ticket must be updated with the resolution steps and marked closed. A post-incident review is mandatory for all Severity 1 incidents and must be completed within 3 business days. The review must identify the root cause, contributing factors, and action items with owners and due dates.

This document defines how employees should report technical issues, bugs, and operational problems that affect systems, tools, or workflows. All issues must be logged in the issue tracking system. Issues reported verbally, via messaging channels, or by email without a corresponding ticket are not considered formally reported and will not be assigned for resolution. Every issue ticket must include a clear description of the problem, the steps taken to reproduce it, the environment or system affected, the observed and expected behavior, and the impact on work. Issues are categorized by type: system outage, performance degradation, data error, access failure, or general bug. Categorization must be applied at the time of submission and determines the routing of the ticket. Misclassified tickets will be re-routed but may experience delays. Priority levels are assigned by the team lead or support manager after initial review. Employees should not set their own priority to urgent unless the issue is causing a complete work stoppage for multiple people. Inflating priority without justification will result in the ticket being downgraded. Once submitted, the reporter is responsible for responding to clarifying questions within one business day. This document defines the rules and procedures for requesting and approving employee leave. It applies to all full-time and part-time employees. Employees are entitled to 20 days of paid annual leave per calendar year. Leave accrues monthly at 1.67 days per month and does not carry over beyond 5 unused days into the next calendar year. Any unused days above that threshold are forfeited at year-end. Sick leave is provided separately at 10 days per year. Sick leave does not accrue and does not carry over. A medical certificate is required for any sick leave exceeding 3 consecutive days. To request leave, an employee must submit a leave request through the HR portal at least 5 business days in advance for planned leave. Emergency or unplanned leave must be reported to the direct manager by 9:00 AM on the day of absence, followed by a formal HR portal submission upon return. Leave requests require manager approval. Managers must respond within 2 business days. Approval may be declined if the requested period conflicts with a critical project deadline, a team coverage minimum, or a previously approved leave from another team member in the same function. Unpaid leave may be granted at manager and HR discretion for personal circumstances not covered by standard entitlements. Requests must be submitted in writing with a stated reason and expected duration. Public holidays are separate from annual leave and are not deducted from the employee leave balance. Employees required to work on a public holiday are entitled to a compensatory day off to be taken within 30 days. Leave records are maintained in the HR system and are accessible to both the employee and their direct manager at any time.

This document describes the steps taken to integrate a new employee into the company during their first 30 days. It applies to all full-time hires across all departments. Before the employee's start date, the hiring manager must submit a system access request for all required tools and platforms through the IT portal. Equipment must be ordered at least 5 business days before the start date. A buddy must be assigned from within the team to provide informal guidance during the first two weeks. On the first day, IT will provide the employee with their device, credentials, and access to core systems. The HR team will conduct a 90-minute session covering company policies, benefits, and compliance requirements. The employee must complete mandatory compliance training modules by the end of week one. During week one, the hiring manager is responsible for conducting a team introduction meeting, providing an of the team's scope, current priorities, and ways of working. The manager must also schedule recurring one-on-one meetings and clarify the performance expectations for the first 90 days. By the end of week two, the employee must have read-only access to the primary codebase or operational systems relevant to their role, with full working

schedule recurring one-on-one meetings and clarify the performance expectations for the first 90 days. By the end of week two, the employee must have read-only access to the primary codebase or operational systems relevant to their role, with full working access granted once the manager confirms readiness. The buddy is responsible for answering day-to-day questions and introducing the employee to relevant colleagues. At the end of week four, the hiring manager must conduct a formal check-in to review progress against onboarding goals, address any blockers, and confirm that outstanding access or tooling gaps are resolved. A brief written summary of this check-in must be filed in the HR system.

This document defines the end-to-end process for planning, preparing, and executing a software release. It applies to all product and platform teams. A release cycle begins with a planning meeting held at the start of each sprint or milestone period. During this meeting, the team confirms the scope of the release, identifies dependencies, and flags any risks. A release lead is assigned for each release and is responsible for coordinating the process from planning to post-release confirmation. Once development is complete, the release lead creates a release candidate branch from the main branch and opens a release tracking ticket. This ticket must list all included changes, the target release date, the deployment window, the rollback plan, and the names of the engineers responsible for deployment. A release candidate must be deployed to the staging environment and undergo a minimum of one full regression test cycle before production deployment is considered. Results of the regression test must be documented in the release ticket. Any blocker issues found in staging must be resolved before the release proceeds. Non-blocker issues must be documented and accepted in writing by the product lead. The production deployment follows the deployment process defined in the deployment policy.

The production deployment follows the deployment process defined in the deployment policy. After deployment, the release lead must verify that all included features and fixes are functioning as expected in production before closing the release ticket. A release summary must be posted in the internal changelog within one business day of a successful release. The summary must include the release version, the date, a brief description of changes, and a link to the full change log. Releases that are rolled back must have a separate incident ticket opened immediately and a post-mortem completed within 3 business days.

This document outlines the rules and expectations for employees working remotely on a full-time, hybrid, or occasional basis. Hybrid employees are required to be present in the office a minimum of 3 days per week. The specific days must be agreed with the direct manager and kept consistent unless operationally adjusted. Office attendance is mandatory on days when all-hands meetings, onboarding sessions, or client visits are scheduled. Employees working remotely must maintain the same availability and responsiveness as they would in the office. This includes being reachable via the designated communication platform during core hours of 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM and joining scheduled video calls with camera enabled unless a valid exception is communicated in advance. All remote work must be performed from a secure location. Employees must not work from public Wi-Fi without an active VPN connection. Company devices must be used for all work-related tasks. Use of personal devices to access company systems remotely is permitted only through the approved virtual desktop environment. Employees are responsible for maintaining a suitable and distraction-free work environment. The company does not provide home office equipment beyond what is issued at the time of hire. The company does not provide home office equipment beyond what is issued at the time of hire. A one-time remote work setup allowance is available to eligible employees, subject to manager and finance approval. Remote work is not a substitute for personal leave. Employees who are unwell should take sick leave rather than work remotely. Remote work privileges may be suspended if the employee consistently fails to meet performance expectations, communication standards, or security requirements. Any suspension will be communicated in writing by the manager with a stated review period.

This document defines the mandatory security practices that all employees must follow to protect company systems, data, and infrastructure. All employees must use strong passwords of at least 14 characters, combining uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols. Passwords must not be reused across systems and must be changed every 90 days. A password manager approved by the IT department must be used to store credentials. Multi-factor authentication is mandatory for all accounts that access company systems, including email, cloud infrastructure, internal tools, and third-party services where supported. Requests to disable MFA will not be approved. Company devices must have full disk encryption enabled at all times. Employees must lock their screen whenever leaving their workstation unattended. Devices must not be left unattended in public spaces. Sensitive data must not be stored on personal devices, personal cloud storage, or any system not managed by IT. Data classified as confidential or restricted must be handled only within approved internal systems and must not be transmitted via personal email or consumer messaging apps. Employees must not install unapproved software on company devices. All software installations require a request through the IT portal. Unauthorized software may be removed without notice. must not be transmitted via personal email or consumer messaging apps. Employees must not install unapproved software on company devices. Phishing or suspicious emails must be reported to the security team immediately using the designated reporting tool and must not be forwarded, clicked, or replied to. Any suspected security incident, including lost or stolen devices, must be reported to IT within one hour of discovery. Failure to comply with this policy may result in disciplinary action, including revocation of system access.

This document describes the standard toolset available to employees and the process for managing access to those tools. All employees are provisioned with a standard set of tools on their first day, including the company email platform, internal communication tool, project management system, document collaboration suite, and VPN client. Access to these tools is configured automatically based on the employee's department and role profile. No separate request is needed for standard toolset provisioning. Role-specific tools such as the source code repository, CI/CD pipeline, cloud infrastructure consoles, data platforms, and monitoring dashboards are provisioned separately. Access to these tools requires a request submitted through the IT portal with manager approval. The assigned access level is determined by job function and follows the principle of least privilege. Employees must use only company-approved tools for work-related tasks. Using personal accounts or consumer versions of productivity software to store, share, or process work data is not permitted. A current list of approved tools is maintained in the internal IT knowledge base and is updated quarterly. Tool licenses are monitored and reviewed every 6 months. Unused licenses may be revoked without prior notice. Employees who require a tool that is not on the approved list

Employees who require a tool that is not on the approved list must submit a software request through the IT portal, including a business justification and estimated cost. Procurement decisions are made by IT in coordination with the relevant department head. Shared credentials or team accounts for any tool are not permitted. Each employee must have their own individual account. If a tool does not support individual accounts, the IT team must be consulted before use. When an employee leaves or changes roles, all tool access is reviewed and adjusted as part of the standard offboarding or role transition process.

This document defines the standard working hours, attendance expectations, and overtime guidelines for all employees. Standard working hours are 9:00 AM to 6:00 PM, Monday through Friday, with a one-hour unpaid lunch break, resulting in an 8-hour working day and a 40-hour working week. Core hours, during which all employees are expected to be available for meetings and collaboration, are 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM. Flexible start and end times are permitted within a window of 8:00 AM to 7:00 PM, provided the employee completes 8 hours per day and is available during core hours. Flexible arrangements must be agreed upon with the direct manager and documented in the HR system. Attendance is tracked through the time-tracking system. Employees are responsible for logging their hours accurately on a daily basis. Timesheets must be submitted by end of day each Friday for the current week. Overtime is defined as any hours worked beyond 40 per week. Overtime must be pre-approved by the direct manager. Approved overtime is compensated either as additional pay at 1.5 times the standard hourly rate or as equivalent time off in lieu, to be taken within the same calendar month.
